headline: Doña Oscarina: How One Woman Wove Indigenous Science Into Global Climate Action

summary_short: Doña Oscarina brought women's agricultural expertise into environmental monitoring, cultivating 18 cassava varieties while preserving ceramic and medicinal plant knowled…
body:
When Doña Oscarina Caldas Azevedo asked permission to gather clay, she addressed Grandmother Clay—Di'i Mahso in the Desana language—with reverence and obligation. For decades, this master ceramicist, farmer, and environmental researcher lived this principle: that Indigenous cosmology, women's agricultural knowledge, and modern climate science were not separate domains but one interconnected system. When she died on July 4th in her home community of Cunuri in Brazil's upper Rio Negro region, she left behind a model for how communities can document and defend ecological wisdom. As the first woman to serve as an Indigenous Environmental Management Agent on the Tiquié River, Oscarina changed what environmental monitoring could measure. She argued that men and women worked in different places and observed different parts of the agricultural cycle. Without women's knowledge, she insisted, a network would miss critical information from fields, gardens, kitchens, and food preparation. Colleagues remembered her speaking firmly and expecting her expertise to be treated seriously—her presence altered how the entire network understood their work.

During her AIMA work, Oscarina and her husband Rafael monitored crop cycles, rainfall, and river levels while she kept detailed diaries blending observation with reflection. She cultivated 18 varieties of cassava, understanding how each responded to soil, weather, and care. But her ambitions extended far beyond her fields. She contributed to research journals, visited the British Museum and Kew Gardens, attended the International Congress of Ethnobiology, and spoke at COP30 in Belém about climate change and Indigenous political struggles. Those who heard her speak described a diplomat capable of moving between cultures while remaining direct about her beliefs—someone who could explain difficult ideas without making listeners feel foolish.

Oscarina's legacy reveals a quiet truth: the knowledge that will help communities adapt to climate change has often been preserved by women, documented in diaries and demonstrated through daily practice, waiting only to be heard by those willing to listen.
